notes.A: An initiator causes the lasting initial genetic alteration in the classical model.
notes.B: Mismatch repair corrects replication errors and does not refer to stimulation of an initiated clone.
notes.D: A telomerase inhibitor is defined by its effect on maintenance of chromosome ends.
notes.E: Proofreading is a mechanism that removes certain misincorporated bases during DNA synthesis.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes the spread of malignant tumour cells to distant organs?
questions.why: Metastasis requires local invasion, dissemination through a route such as blood or lymph, and colonisation of a distant tissue. The final step requires survival and growth in a new environment.

notes.A: Mitosis, transcription and translation are ordinary cellular processes that can occur without tumour spread.
notes.B: Replication and splicing are processes of genome duplication and RNA processing, respectively.
notes.C: Repair, arrest and apoptosis are potential responses to damage within a cell.
notes.D: Antigen recognition and phagocytosis are immune processes and do not define the steps of tumour spread.

questions.stem: A mutation in a DNA-repair gene can raise cancer risk principally by:

options.label: E
options.text: Eliminating the need for DNA replication

questions.why: A damaging mutation in a repair gene can let normally corrected DNA lesions persist. When copied or misrepaired, some lesions become mutations that can affect genes controlling growth and survival.

notes.B: A repair defect may affect how a cell transcribes damaged DNA, but the general cancer risk stems from genome instability.
notes.C: Cytokine receptors use signalling pathways distinct from the core function of repairing DNA lesions.
notes.D: Stability of a collagen triple helix is determined by the collagen protein and its processing.
notes.E: Cells still need to replicate their genomes before normal division, even when a repair pathway is defective.

questions.stem: Which virus is strongly linked to malignant transformation in cervical carcinoma?
questions.why: Persistent infection with a high-risk type of human papillomavirus can disrupt normal growth control in cervical epithelium. It is the major cause of cervical carcinoma.

notes.A: Influenza A is a respiratory virus and is not an established cause of cervical carcinoma.
notes.B: Rhinovirus is a common cause of upper respiratory infections and lacks this established cancer association.
notes.C: Norovirus is typically associated with acute gastroenteritis.
notes.E: Rotavirus is an important cause of acute diarrhoeal disease, particularly in young children.

questions.stem: Which virus is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma in chronic infection?
questions.why: Chronic hepatitis B increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma through prolonged liver injury, among other mechanisms. The association is with persistent infection.

notes.A: Epstein–Barr virus is associated with certain lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, among other cancers.
notes.C: Influenza A is primarily a respiratory pathogen with no comparable established link to chronic carcinogenic hepatitis.
notes.D: Rhinovirus is a common cause of upper respiratory tract infection.
notes.E: Rotavirus is chiefly associated with acute gastroenteritis rather than chronic liver injury.

questions.stem: Which molecular feature permits a cell to pause division when DNA damage is detected?

options.label: B
options.text: Random loss of the mitochondrial genome

questions.why: DNA damage can trigger checkpoints that inhibit cell-cycle progression, allowing time for repair before division. Persistent or severe damage may instead lead to senescence or apoptosis.

notes.A: Loss of all ribosomes would prevent normal protein synthesis and is not a regulated response to DNA damage.
notes.B: Loss of mitochondrial DNA impairs mitochondrial function and is not the mechanism that checks nuclear DNA before division.
notes.D: Unrestricted cyclin activity can drive progression through checkpoints rather than impose a pause.
notes.E: Constitutive oncogene activation commonly favours growth signalling instead of providing a regulated DNA damage checkpoint.

questions.stem: What is the principal function of a restriction endonuclease in recombinant DNA technology?

options.label: A
options.text: Join DNA ends into phosphodiester bonds

options.label: B
options.text: Transcribe selected genes into messenger RNA

options.label: D
options.text: Cut DNA at specific recognition sequences

options.label: E
options.text: Replicate a plasmid without host cells

questions.why: A restriction endonuclease recognises a particular motif in DNA and cleaves at or near that motif. Sequence recognition explains why different restriction enzymes cut different sites.

notes.A: DNA ligase is the enzyme that seals a break in the sugar-phosphate backbone.
notes.B: RNA polymerase is responsible for transcribing a gene into RNA.
notes.C: Ribosomes translate messenger RNA into a polypeptide rather than directly reading DNA.
notes.E: Plasmid DNA replication requires DNA synthesis machinery. Cleaving DNA is a separate activity.

questions.stem: Which enzyme covalently joins DNA fragments to form a recombinant DNA molecule?
questions.why: DNA ligase creates a phosphodiester bond across a nick in the DNA backbone. This covalently joins adjacent DNA ends.

notes.A: DNA helicase is responsible for separating paired nucleic acid strands.
notes.C: Primase makes a short RNA primer and does not seal DNA ends together.
notes.D: Topoisomerase reshapes DNA topology by transient cleavage and resealing, rather than joining separate fragments into a stable product.
notes.E: Reverse transcriptase is an RNA-directed DNA polymerase and does not seal nicks.

questions.stem: What is the primary advantage of compatible sticky ends in DNA cloning?

options.label: A
options.text: They prevent base pairing at the cut sites

options.label: B
options.text: They eliminate the need for a cloning vector

options.label: C
options.text: They block foreign DNA from entering cells

options.label: D
options.text: They automatically create a new promoter

questions.why: Compatible sticky ends have complementary single-stranded overhangs. Base pairing between them can align the fragments, while a separate ligation reaction makes the backbone continuous.

notes.A: Complementarity permits base pairing at the overhangs.
notes.B: Cohesive ends can help align fragments but do not provide a vector's replication functions.
notes.C: Annealing of compatible DNA ends is a property of base pairing and does not inherently block cellular uptake.
notes.D: A promoter requires an appropriate regulatory sequence, which is not guaranteed by joining cohesive ends.

questions.stem: Why can a bacterial restriction–modification system spare the host's own genome?

options.label: B
options.text: The host genome contains only RNA

options.label: D
options.text: DNA ligase is absent from bacterial cells

questions.why: In a typical restriction–modification system, a methyltransferase marks the bacterium's DNA at the relevant sequence. The paired restriction enzyme ordinarily cuts unmodified versions of that site.

notes.B: A bacterial chromosome consists of DNA, which can contain sites recognised by restriction enzymes.
notes.C: Recognition sites can occur in bacterial DNA, which is why chemical protection from the matching enzyme matters.
notes.D: Bacterial cells use DNA ligase in processes including replication and repair.
notes.E: A restriction endonuclease recognises a DNA motif as its substrate. It is not a protein-cleaving enzyme.

questions.stem: Which property makes a bacterial plasmid useful as a cloning vector?

options.label: B
options.text: An absence of selectable genetic markers

questions.why: A plasmid origin of replication lets the plasmid be copied as a distinct DNA molecule in a compatible host. The origin is recognised by replication machinery.

notes.A: Bacteria lack a membrane-bound nucleus, so a human nuclear envelope is irrelevant.
notes.B: Selectable genetic markers are commonly useful features of a cloning vector.
notes.D: Plasmids are DNA molecules that do not require permanent attachment to protein-synthesising ribosomes.
notes.E: Human telomerase extends the ends of linear chromosomes and is unnecessary for a typical circular bacterial plasmid.

questions.stem: Why is an antibiotic-resistance marker useful on a cloning plasmid?

options.label: A
options.text: It cuts inserted DNA at exact loci

options.label: B
options.text: It synthesizes the protein of interest

options.label: D
options.text: It permits selection of transformed cells

options.label: E
options.text: It supplies RNA primers for PCR

questions.why: The resistance marker is a selectable trait: it distinguishes cells carrying the plasmid from susceptible cells by their response to the relevant antibiotic. The marker and the gene being studied serve separate functions.

notes.A: DNA cleavage at specific sites is a restriction enzyme function.
notes.B: Production of a target protein depends on expression of its coding region rather than the marker's role in selection.
notes.C: Resistance is a specific trait and does not supply protection against all mutations.
notes.E: PCR uses DNA primers, which are distinct from a plasmid's selectable marker.

questions.stem: A cloning vector can replicate in both E. coli and yeast. Such a vector is termed a:
questions.why: A shuttle vector can be propagated in two different host types. It contains replication features recognised by the respective hosts.

notes.A: A cosmid is defined by the presence of phage cos sites and is not necessarily compatible with two hosts.
notes.C: A capsid is the protein shell of a virus, rather than a vector defined by dual host compatibility.
notes.D: A restriction site is a short sequence recognised by an enzyme and does not define the host range of a vector.
notes.E: A reporter or probe is used to detect an event or target, rather than to define a vector's ability to propagate in two hosts.

questions.stem: Which vector is especially suitable for cloning very large genomic DNA fragments?
questions.why: A bacterial artificial chromosome is a vector designed to maintain much larger genomic inserts than an ordinary cloning plasmid. This capacity makes it suitable for retaining long contiguous regions.

notes.B: A conventional small plasmid has a more limited insert capacity.
notes.C: A transient expression plasmid is selected for short-term expression rather than for maintaining very large genomic fragments.
notes.D: A phagemid combines features of a plasmid and a phage but is not typically used for inserts as large as those a BAC can maintain.
notes.E: A PCR primer is a short starting strand for polymerase and is not a vector for maintaining genomic DNA.

questions.stem: What is the defining difference between cDNA and a genomic copy of a mature eukaryotic protein-coding gene?

options.label: B
options.text: Genomic DNA is devoid of introns

questions.why: Complementary DNA derived from a mature mRNA reflects the splice pattern of that transcript. Introns present in the genomic copy are usually absent from the cDNA.

notes.A: Centromeres are chromosomal structures and do not typically appear in cDNA copied from a processed protein-coding transcript.
notes.B: Genomic DNA may contain both introns and exons at a gene.
notes.D: Telomeric repeats occur at chromosome ends and are not a defining feature of cDNA.
notes.E: Genomic DNA can serve as a template for amplification.

questions.stem: Which enzyme produces complementary DNA using an RNA template?
questions.why: Reverse transcriptase catalyses DNA synthesis on an RNA template. The resulting complementary DNA follows the sequence of the copied RNA.

notes.A: DNA ligase creates backbone bonds between adjacent DNA ends and does not copy an RNA template.
notes.B: DNA gyrase is a bacterial topoisomerase that changes DNA supercoiling.
notes.C: RNA polymerase II transcribes DNA into RNA rather than synthesising DNA from RNA.
notes.E: A restriction endonuclease is a sequence-specific DNA-cutting enzyme.

questions.stem: Why is cDNA particularly useful for expressing a human protein in an ordinary E. coli host?

options.label: B
options.text: It lacks introns requiring eukaryotic splicing

options.label: C
options.text: It automatically folds all mammalian proteins

options.label: D
options.text: It does not require any bacterial promoter

questions.why: A cDNA copy of mature human mRNA usually has its coding exons joined. Ordinary E. coli lacks the spliceosome that would remove typical human introns, so a continuous coding sequence avoids that processing requirement.

notes.A: A human centromere is used in chromosome segregation and is not needed to read the coding sequence in a bacterium.
notes.C: A continuous coding sequence does not guarantee proper folding or processing of every human protein.
notes.D: Transcription in E. coli still requires a promoter recognised by bacterial transcription machinery.
notes.E: A cDNA coding sequence cannot itself prevent degradation of the expressed protein.

questions.stem: Which material is represented in a genomic DNA library but may be absent from a tissue-specific cDNA library?
questions.why: A genomic library represents DNA from across the genome, including intervening and intergenic regions. A tissue cDNA library represents the RNAs copied from that tissue, so sequences absent from those RNAs are generally missing.

notes.A: Expressed messenger RNA sequences can be represented in the cDNA library as DNA copies.
notes.B: Coding exons incorporated into expressed transcripts can be present in both kinds of library.
notes.C: Protein-coding transcripts are among the main sequences represented in a typical mRNA-derived cDNA library.
notes.D: Ribosomal RNA representation depends on RNA selection, so it is not the defining difference from a genomic library.

questions.stem: Which process is repeated during each basic PCR amplification cycle?
questions.why: In one PCR cycle the DNA strands separate, primers pair with complementary sites and DNA polymerase extends the primers. Repeating these events increases copies of the target.

notes.B: Translation makes protein, splicing processes RNA and ligation joins adjacent nucleic acid ends.
notes.C: Transcription and secretion involve making RNA and exporting cellular products, respectively, neither of which is required for PCR.
notes.D: Glycosylation, hydroxylation and folding are examples of protein processing events.
notes.E: Fragmentation, staining and imaging may be used in analysis but are not the repeating DNA copying steps.

questions.stem: What occurs in the primer-annealing step of PCR?
questions.why: Annealing is the association of primers with complementary sequences on the separated template strands. A paired primer can then provide the starting end for DNA synthesis.

notes.A: A thermostable polymerase remains usable during repeated PCR cycles rather than being irreversibly inactivated at annealing.
notes.B: Translation is ribosome-mediated synthesis of a polypeptide from RNA.
notes.C: Restriction enzymes are DNA-cleaving enzymes and are not required to join DNA during annealing.
notes.E: PCR occurs in a cell-free reaction, so plasmid entry into cells is irrelevant to primer annealing.

questions.stem: What is the principal molecular event during the PCR extension stage?
questions.why: During extension, DNA polymerase adds complementary deoxyribonucleotides to the paired primer's free 3′ end. This produces a new strand complementary to the template.

notes.A: Ligase seals backbone nicks and does not carry out chain elongation.
notes.C: Primers supply a starting end for polymerase and do not cleave duplex DNA.
notes.D: Ribosomes make polypeptides and have no role in the DNA extension reaction.
notes.E: Spliceosomes remove introns from RNA, not intervening regions of a DNA template.

questions.stem: Why is a thermostable DNA polymerase used in repeated PCR cycles?

options.label: A
options.text: It directly synthesizes protein from DNA

questions.why: A thermostable DNA polymerase remains active through many rounds of heating to separate DNA strands. The same enzyme can therefore support repeated extensions.

notes.A: DNA polymerase synthesises DNA. Protein synthesis is performed by ribosomes.
notes.B: Extension requires deoxyribonucleotide substrates as building blocks for the new DNA strand.
notes.C: Polymerase requires a primer to provide a pre-existing 3′ end.
notes.D: Thermostability refers to enzyme activity after heating and does not ensure a contamination-free reaction.

questions.stem: In ideal PCR with 100% efficiency, ten complete cycles generate approximately how many copies from one starting target?
questions.why: Each full cycle ideally doubles the number of copies, so starting from one gives 2 to the power of 10 after 10 cycles. The result is 1,024 copies under the stated assumption.

notes.B: A total of 100 is not the result of doubling the starting amount 10 times.
notes.C: A total of 256 is reached after eight ideal doublings.
notes.D: A total of 512 is reached after nine ideal doublings.
notes.E: A total of 2,048 is reached after eleven ideal doublings.

questions.stem: Which reagent pair chiefly determines which DNA region will be amplified in conventional PCR?
questions.why: Forward and reverse primers bind complementary sites on opposite strands. Their binding sites specify the two boundaries of the amplified region.

notes.A: Magnesium and other salts can affect polymerase activity and binding conditions but cannot specify a unique target sequence.
notes.B: Loading dye and agarose are used to analyse DNA by electrophoresis.
notes.D: Antibiotic selection is a way to distinguish cells with a selectable trait, rather than a way to delimit a region of DNA for copying.
notes.E: DNA stains and illumination can help visualise products after amplification but do not select the target sequence.

questions.stem: Why does DNA migrate toward the positive electrode during electrophoresis?

options.label: A
options.text: Its bases have a net positive charge

options.label: B
options.text: DNA fragments carry more positive charges than RNA

options.label: D
options.text: Its phosphate backbone is negatively charged

options.label: E
options.text: Its deoxyribose units bind the anode

questions.why: Ionised phosphate groups give DNA a net negative charge under typical electrophoresis conditions. The electric field draws the molecules towards the positive electrode.

notes.A: The phosphate backbone, rather than a net positive charge on the bases, is responsible for the direction of migration.
notes.B: Both DNA and RNA have negatively charged phosphate backbones.
notes.C: Histones are basic proteins and are not the basis of migration of purified DNA in a standard gel.
notes.E: Deoxyribose is a sugar in the backbone. Its role is structural rather than determining attraction to the positive electrode.

questions.stem: In a standard agarose gel, which linear DNA fragment normally travels farther in a given time?
questions.why: Agarose forms a molecular sieve. Smaller linear DNA fragments pass more readily through its pores, so they usually migrate farther than larger linear fragments under the same conditions.

notes.A: Larger linear fragments experience more resistance passing through the gel pores.
notes.C: GC content is not the main determinant of mobility in ordinary size separation of linear DNA.
notes.D: Adenine content does not usually determine migration distance above the effect of fragment size.
notes.E: Standard agarose sizing compares purified DNA fragments, not the number of histones bound to them.

questions.stem: Which blotting technique detects particular DNA sequences after electrophoretic separation?
questions.why: A Southern blot transfers DNA fragments to a membrane after separation. A complementary nucleic acid probe can identify the fragment containing the target DNA sequence.

notes.A: A Northern blot is used to detect RNA sequences following separation and transfer to a membrane.
notes.B: A Western blot uses antibodies to detect specific proteins.
notes.C: A far-Western blot is used to study protein–protein binding.
notes.D: A dot blot applies material directly to a membrane rather than separating the fragments by electrophoresis first.

questions.stem: Which blotting technique is traditionally used to detect a specific RNA transcript?
questions.why: Northern blotting separates RNA, transfers it to a membrane and identifies the transcript by recognising a complementary sequence. The position of a band also gives information about transcript size.

notes.B: A Southern blot uses a nucleic acid probe to recognise particular DNA fragments rather than RNA transcripts.
notes.C: A Western blot primarily detects proteins via antibody binding.
notes.D: A protein immunoblot uses antibodies to detect a protein target rather than an RNA transcript.
notes.E: Restriction mapping describes cleavage sites or fragment sizes in DNA rather than detecting a specific RNA.

questions.stem: Which blotting method primarily detects specific proteins using antibodies?
questions.why: A Western blot separates proteins and transfers them to a membrane. An antibody specific for the target protein can reveal the band corresponding to it.

notes.A: A Southern blot uses a complementary probe to detect a DNA sequence.
notes.B: A Northern blot is a method for detecting a specific RNA.
notes.D: A restriction map shows enzyme cleavage sites in DNA and does not detect a protein on a membrane.
notes.E: DNA sequencing is used to determine the order of nucleotides.

questions.stem: Which DNA variation makes restriction-fragment-length polymorphism analysis possible?

options.label: C
options.text: Complete identity of all tandem repeats

options.label: E
options.text: Conversion of DNA into messenger RNA

questions.why: A sequence variant can create or abolish a restriction site, or alter the length between fixed sites. The resulting restriction fragments then differ in length and can distinguish alleles.

notes.A: A uniform sequence would give no sequence-based polymorphism in restriction fragment lengths.
notes.B: Restriction enzymes are needed to reveal cleavage fragment sizes in conventional RFLP analysis.
notes.C: Identical tandem repeat lengths cannot by themselves create a length polymorphism.
notes.E: Transcribing DNA into RNA is a separate process from cutting DNA into diagnostic fragments.

questions.stem: Why must primer-binding sequences be known before routine targeted PCR is designed?

options.label: C
options.text: To remove the requirement for DNA template

options.label: D
options.text: To eliminate the chance of contamination

options.label: E
options.text: To amplify the chosen DNA segment

questions.why: Targeted PCR depends on the primers recognising the intended template. Information about the flanking sequence allows the primers to define the segment copied.

notes.A: A primer's main role is to initiate synthesis on a complementary template. PCR does not correct mutations already present in the target.
notes.B: Conventional PCR does not rely on restriction digestion, regardless of how the flanking sequence was identified.
notes.C: The template supplies the sequence that polymerase copies. Knowledge of primer-binding sequence cannot replace it.
notes.D: Contamination control is separate from selecting a complementary primer.

questions.stem: Why are retroviral vectors used cautiously in integrating gene therapy?

options.label: A
options.text: Their genomes cannot enter mammalian cells

options.label: C
options.text: Insertion may disrupt or activate host genes

options.label: D
options.text: They lack any nucleic acid cargo

questions.why: Integration is one way to maintain therapeutic sequences as cells divide. If insertion alters the activity of a host gene, it can produce unwanted effects, including clonal expansion.

notes.A: Delivery into mammalian cells is a property these therapeutic vectors are designed to provide.
notes.B: Gene transfer into target cells is distinct from giving a patient preformed antibodies.
notes.D: The vector carries genetic material whose insertion is the source of this risk.
notes.E: The ability to maintain an integrated sequence is a reason to use this type of vector and is also why effects of insertion matter.

questions.stem: Which biotechnological application best illustrates manufacturing a therapeutic protein using engineered microbes?

options.label: A
options.text: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

questions.why: Recombinant human insulin is a therapeutic protein produced by cells expressing a human insulin coding sequence. It illustrates manufacture by a production organism rather than extraction from a donor.

notes.A: Red-cell transfusion uses cells collected from donors.
notes.B: An autologous graft is tissue taken from the patient's own body.
notes.C: Centrifugation is a physical separation method and does not produce a recombinant protein.
notes.E: Purifying urinary electrolytes is chemical separation of small ions, not protein production.

questions.stem: What is a principal challenge in ex vivo gene transfer to patient cells?

options.label: A
options.text: Absence of RNA inside all human cells

options.label: E
options.text: Inability to culture any human cells

questions.why: Ex vivo transfer modifies a patient's cells outside the body. A practical challenge is obtaining enough viable cells with the intended modification and acceptable safety and expression profiles.

notes.A: Human cells contain RNA needed for normal expression of genes.
notes.C: Susceptibility to vector delivery differs by cell type and vector, rather than being universally absent.
notes.D: A therapeutic modification may be intended to change expression. Unwanted effects on expression are also possible.
notes.E: Many types of human cells can be cultured under suitable conditions.

questions.stem: Which test strategy detects a known single-base mutation by sequence-specific probe hybridization?
questions.why: An allele-specific probe is designed to distinguish sequences that differ at a known base. Complementary binding reports which allele the sample contains.

notes.A: Serum protein electrophoresis measures patterns of separated proteins and does not directly identify a particular DNA base.
notes.B: Osmotic fragility testing assesses red-cell lysis in hypotonic conditions. It does not identify an individual nucleotide.
notes.C: Platelet agglutination is a cellular response measured in some assays, rather than evidence that a probe recognised a DNA allele.
notes.D: Trichrome staining distinguishes tissue components, including collagen, in sections.

questions.stem: What is the principal role of a radiolabelled or fluorescent DNA probe in molecular diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Catalyse DNA synthesis on its own

questions.why: A labelled probe binds to a complementary sequence. Its detectable label reveals the presence or position of matching target DNA.

notes.B: DNA synthesis is catalysed by a polymerase. The probe's job here is detection.
notes.C: Translation of mRNA into a peptide is catalysed by a ribosome.
notes.D: A probe can bind a complementary target but does not digest noncoding DNA.
notes.E: The spliceosome is responsible for removal of introns from precursor RNA, rather than from genomic DNA.

questions.stem: Which feature is particularly useful when selecting a DNA cloning vector for downstream protein expression?

options.label: E
options.text: Inability to replicate inside host cells

questions.why: An expression vector has regulatory sequences that function in the chosen host. These allow transcription of the cloned coding sequence and translation of the resulting RNA.

notes.A: A replication origin is generally useful for maintaining a cloning plasmid, though it does not by itself drive expression.
notes.B: A selectable marker can be useful for finding cells that retain the vector.
notes.D: An appropriate translation initiation signal is needed for efficient synthesis of a protein.
notes.E: Lack of replication could limit maintenance of a cloning vector and is not a feature that enables expression.

questions.stem: Which enzyme deficiency causes the classic Lesch–Nyhan syndrome?
questions.why: HGPRT recycles hypoxanthine and guanine into IMP and GMP using PRPP. Severe loss of this salvage activity favours urate overproduction and causes classic Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.

notes.A: APRT salvages adenine. Its deficiency is associated with 2,8-dihydroxyadenine stone disease.
notes.B: CPS II is part of pyrimidine synthesis and does not salvage purines.
notes.C: Xanthine oxidase is involved in urate formation. Loss of its activity can cause xanthinuria.
notes.D: Adenosine deaminase deficiency can cause severe combined immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: A child with excessive urate production, neurological abnormalities and self-injurious behaviour most likely has:
questions.why: Severe HGPRT deficiency combines urate overproduction with a characteristic neurological and behavioural disorder. Self-injury in a child with this metabolic pattern strongly supports Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.

notes.A: Hereditary orotic aciduria results from impaired UMP formation and has a characteristic pyrimidine abnormality.
notes.C: Von Gierke disease can cause hyperuricaemia, but its core finding is defective glucose release with fasting hypoglycaemia.
notes.D: Maple syrup urine disease involves impaired branched-chain amino acid catabolism.
notes.E: Familial hypercholesterolaemia causes elevated LDL cholesterol and premature atherosclerotic risk.

questions.stem: Why does severe adenosine deaminase deficiency damage lymphocyte development?

options.label: E
options.text: Increased catabolism of uracil into beta-alanine

questions.why: With severe ADA deficiency, deoxyadenosine accumulates and can be converted to excess dATP. This disrupts ribonucleotide reductase and deoxynucleotide balance, to which developing lymphocytes are particularly vulnerable.

notes.A: The direct block involves purine nucleoside degradation rather than formation of pyrimidine rings.
notes.B: Mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate is involved in urea synthesis.
notes.C: Collagen cross-linking occurs in the extracellular matrix and does not explain lymphocyte toxicity from ADA loss.
notes.E: Uracil breakdown is a separate pyrimidine catabolic pathway.

questions.stem: A patient with ADA deficiency has severe recurrent infections in infancy. Which immune diagnosis is most consistent?
questions.why: Severe ADA deficiency impairs lymphocyte development and survival through accumulation of purine metabolites. Loss of effective T- and B-cell immunity accounts for the severe, recurrent infections of SCID.

notes.B: Neutrophil elastase-related congenital neutropenia is a disorder of myeloid cells and is distinct from ADA-related lymphocyte deficiency.
notes.C: Anaphylaxis is an immediate hypersensitivity reaction rather than a combined deficiency of adaptive immunity.
notes.D: Factor VIII deficiency is a coagulation disorder that causes bleeding.
notes.E: Vitamin K malabsorption can impair coagulation factor function but does not explain combined lymphocyte deficiency.

questions.stem: Which drug reduces uric acid production by inhibiting xanthine oxidase?
questions.why: Allopurinol is converted to oxypurinol. Inhibition of xanthine oxidoreductase reduces oxidation of hypoxanthine and xanthine towards urate.

notes.A: Azathioprine is a precursor of 6-mercaptopurine and acts through thiopurine metabolites.
notes.B: Methotrexate is an antifolate that interferes with nucleotide biosynthesis, rather than inhibiting the terminal steps of purine degradation.
notes.D: Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, reducing deoxynucleotide synthesis.
notes.E: Trimethoprim is an inhibitor of bacterial dihydrofolate reductase rather than xanthine oxidase.

questions.stem: What is the immediate effect of xanthine oxidase inhibition on purine degradation?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased conversion of guanine into GMP

options.label: B
options.text: Increased salvage of thymine to TMP

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced degradation of uracil to beta-alanine

options.label: E
options.text: Reduced conversion of xanthine to urate

questions.why: Xanthine oxidase activity is responsible for the last oxidation step in human purine degradation, from xanthine to urate. Inhibiting the enzyme reduces that conversion directly.

notes.A: Conversion of guanine to GMP is catalysed by HGPRT in the purine salvage pathway.
notes.B: Thymine is a pyrimidine base, outside the purine degradation pathway.
notes.C: Uracil degradation to beta-alanine is part of pyrimidine breakdown.
notes.D: Carbamoyl phosphate is made by carbamoyl phosphate synthetases, independently of terminal purine oxidation.

questions.stem: Why can excessive PRPP availability favour hyperuricaemia?

options.label: A
options.text: It destroys renal urate transporters directly

options.label: B
options.text: It drives increased de novo purine synthesis

options.label: C
options.text: It prevents formation of all pyrimidines

options.label: D
options.text: It converts uric acid back into inosine

options.label: E
options.text: It blocks the xanthine oxidase reaction

questions.why: PRPP is a substrate and a positive regulator of the committed step of purine biosynthesis. Greater production of purine nucleotides can increase the substrate eventually degraded to urate.

notes.A: The effect described is on purine production, rather than direct injury to renal urate transporters.
notes.C: PRPP is also used in pyrimidine synthesis when orotate is converted to OMP.
notes.D: Humans do not use PRPP to reverse uric acid degradation back to inosine.
notes.E: Xanthine oxidase acts downstream in degradation. PRPP affects substrate generation, not inhibition of that enzyme.

questions.stem: Which inflammatory deposit is characteristic of acute gout?
questions.why: Monosodium urate can crystallise in joints when local conditions favour precipitation. These crystals trigger the acute inflammatory response of gout.

notes.A: Calcium oxalate crystals are typical of a common form of kidney stone.
notes.B: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are characteristic of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, which can mimic gout.
notes.C: Cholesterol deposition can occur in other chronic conditions but does not define acute gout.
notes.E: Cystine crystals are associated with cystinuria and urinary stone disease.

questions.stem: Why can hypoxanthine–guanine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency increase purine de novo synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: Less salvage leaves more PRPP available

options.label: B
options.text: It directly synthesizes more xanthine oxidase

options.label: C
options.text: It stimulates DNA ligase to make purines

options.label: D
options.text: It prevents all ribose phosphate formation

options.label: E
options.text: It decreases glutamine supply to the liver

questions.why: HGPRT normally consumes PRPP when it salvages purine bases. Deficiency leaves more PRPP available and reduces inhibitory feedback from salvaged nucleotides, favouring de novo purine synthesis.

notes.B: Greater urate production can arise from more substrate reaching an otherwise existing xanthine oxidase pathway.
notes.C: Ligase seals nucleic acid backbones and does not synthesise purine bases.
notes.D: Ribose phosphate remains available and can supply PRPP through normal metabolism.
notes.E: Purine synthesis uses glutamine as a nitrogen donor. Reduced glutamine supply would not explain increased synthesis.

questions.stem: Which metabolic result explains the neurological and immune phenotype of severe ADA deficiency?

options.label: B
options.text: Excess ornithine blocks the urea cycle

questions.why: Raised dATP disrupts ribonucleotide reductase activity and DNA precursor homeostasis, especially in lymphocytes.

questions.stem: 6-Mercaptopurine must undergo which reaction to form active nucleotide analogues in cells?
questions.why: HGPRT uses PRPP to convert 6-mercaptopurine into thioinosine monophosphate. This is an activation step on the route to thiopurine metabolites that interfere with nucleotide metabolism.

notes.A: Thymidylate synthase is used to make dTMP from dUMP and does not activate the thiopurine base.
notes.B: Prolyl hydroxylases act on protein proline residues, not purine drugs.
notes.C: Lysyl oxidase is involved in extracellular matrix cross-linking and is not a thiopurine salvage enzyme.
notes.D: CPS I uses ammonia to make carbamoyl phosphate in the urea cycle.

questions.stem: Which distinction between mammalian CPS I and CPS II is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: CPS I is cytosolic; CPS II is mitochondrial

options.label: B
options.text: CPS I is mitochondrial; CPS II is cytosolic

options.label: C
options.text: Both enzymes function only in the nucleus

options.label: D
options.text: Both enzymes use only free ammonia

options.label: E
options.text: CPS II functions in the urea cycle

questions.why: CPS I works in mitochondria and uses free ammonia for urea synthesis. CPS II is a cytosolic activity of the CAD enzyme complex that uses glutamine nitrogen for de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

notes.A: The compartments are reversed in this option. CPS I is mitochondrial and CPS II is cytosolic.
notes.C: The reactions occur in the mitochondrial matrix or cytosol, rather than exclusively within the nucleus.
notes.D: Free ammonia is the nitrogen substrate of CPS I, whereas CPS II obtains its nitrogen from glutamine.
notes.E: CPS II supplies carbamoyl phosphate for pyrimidines. The urea-cycle enzyme is CPS I.

questions.stem: Which vaccine formulation component chiefly keeps the product within an acceptable pH range?
questions.why: A buffer resists a shift in pH when small amounts of acid or base are introduced. Maintaining the specified pH can help keep vaccine components stable.

notes.B: An adjuvant helps enhance the immune response to a vaccine antigen.
notes.C: The antigen is the target presented to the immune system.
notes.D: A preservative is used to limit microbial contamination in some formulations, especially multidose products.
notes.E: A surfactant can help limit aggregation or improve dispersion. A buffer is responsible for pH control.

questions.stem: Which component may be added to a vaccine to maintain isotonicity and reduce local irritation?
questions.why: Sodium chloride can be used to adjust the concentration of osmotically active particles. A formulation closer to physiological tonicity reduces osmotic stress on local tissues.

notes.A: Formaldehyde has a role in inactivating certain organisms or toxins during manufacture and is not used to adjust tonicity.
notes.B: Ethidium bromide is a nucleic acid stain rather than a vaccine tonicity agent.
notes.C: Acetic anhydride is a reactive chemical and does not serve this formulation role.
notes.E: Potassium cyanide is toxic and is not a vaccine excipient used to adjust tonicity.

questions.stem: Which vaccine excipient can help stabilize proteins and prevent component separation?
questions.why: Gelatin is a stabiliser in some vaccines. It helps preserve susceptible formulation components through storage, including in some freeze-dried products.

notes.A: Urea can destabilise protein structure at sufficient concentration and is not the standard stabiliser identified here.
notes.C: Heparin is an anticoagulant, not the specified vaccine stabiliser.
notes.D: Thrombin is a clotting enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
notes.E: Histamine is a signalling molecule involved in inflammatory responses.

questions.stem: Why is formaldehyde used in manufacturing some vaccines?

options.label: A
options.text: To increase the virulence of microbes

options.label: B
options.text: To create T-cell receptors in vitro

options.label: C
options.text: To covalently link vaccine antigens to collagen

options.label: D
options.text: To release interferons directly in serum

questions.why: In manufacture of some vaccines, formaldehyde is used to inactivate an organism or detoxify a toxin while preserving useful antigenic properties. The final product can contain trace residual formaldehyde.

notes.A: Inactivation is intended to remove infectivity or toxicity, rather than increase virulence.
notes.B: T-cell receptors are generated by developing lymphocytes, not by formaldehyde treatment.
notes.C: The relevant function is inactivation or detoxification. Linking vaccine antigens to collagen is not its stated purpose.
notes.D: Interferons are immune signalling proteins produced by cells, not released directly by vaccine inactivation.

questions.stem: Which term specifically describes administration of a vaccine as opposed to the broader development of immunity?
questions.why: Vaccination refers to administering a vaccine. Immunisation describes the broader process of acquiring protection, which can follow vaccination.

notes.A: Immunisation describes development or provision of protection and is broader than the administration itself.
notes.B: Seroconversion is development of detectable specific antibodies in the blood.
notes.D: Opsonisation is coating of a target to improve its uptake by phagocytes.
notes.E: Neutralisation is blockade of a pathogen or toxin's activity, often through antibody binding.

questions.stem: How does immunological memory improve vaccine protection upon later pathogen exposure?

options.label: A
options.text: Memory clones respond faster than naïve clones

options.label: B
options.text: All innate receptors acquire rearranged V genes

options.label: C
options.text: All neutrophils survive for the entire lifespan

questions.why: Vaccination generates antigen-specific memory B and T cells. On re-exposure these cells can respond more rapidly than naïve cells, supporting faster antibody and cellular responses.

notes.B: Rearrangement of antigen-receptor genes is a feature of adaptive B and T cells, rather than a change acquired by all innate receptors.
notes.C: Neutrophils are relatively short-lived and do not account for antigen-specific recall across a lifetime.
notes.D: A recall response still requires antigen recognition and activation of relevant cells.
notes.E: Immune memory can persist after the original antigen has been cleared.

questions.stem: Vaccine efficacy is most appropriately estimated in which setting?
questions.why: Efficacy estimates protection under controlled trial conditions, usually by comparing the risk of a specified outcome between vaccinated and comparison groups. The design helps reduce bias and confounding.

notes.A: A population survey may contribute to assessment of real-world effectiveness but is an uncontrolled setting.
notes.B: Stock inventories track supply and contain no comparison of disease rates.
notes.C: Billing records can provide observational data. Alone they do not provide a controlled efficacy comparison.
notes.E: Microscopy can support a laboratory measurement but cannot itself estimate clinical protection in a trial.

questions.stem: Vaccine effectiveness differs from efficacy because effectiveness measures:

options.label: A
options.text: Protection only under ideal trial conditions

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of antigen inside the vial

options.label: D
options.text: Direct antibody affinity measured in vitro

questions.why: Effectiveness measures how well a vaccine protects in routine use. The estimate reflects real-world populations and delivery conditions, whereas efficacy typically comes from a controlled trial.

notes.A: Protection measured under controlled trial conditions gives an efficacy estimate.
notes.C: Presence of antigen is a product property rather than evidence of protection in routine use.
notes.D: Antibody affinity is a molecular measurement and does not directly quantify population protection.
notes.E: Manufacturing method describes the product's origin rather than its real-world impact.

questions.stem: Which programme feature most directly helps maintain vaccine potency before administration?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased duration of vaccine exposure to sunlight

questions.why: A cold chain maintains vaccines within product-specific temperature limits during storage and transport. This protects potency from damage due to excessive warmth or, for susceptible products, freezing.

notes.A: Sunlight can damage some vaccine products and is not protective of potency.
notes.B: Temperature tracking is needed to detect damaging excursions before administration.
notes.C: Sterile technique is essential for safe administration but does not maintain potency in storage.
notes.D: Diluent alone does not provide the vaccine antigen needed for the intended immune response.

questions.stem: How can high vaccination coverage protect some unvaccinated members of a population?

options.label: A
options.text: Direct conversion of their B cells into plasma cells

options.label: B
options.text: Elimination of their need for innate immunity

options.label: D
options.text: Automatic transfer of circulating vaccine antigens

options.label: E
options.text: Replacement of their own T-cell receptors

questions.why: When vaccination reduces acquisition or onward transmission, high coverage can interrupt chains of infection. This lowers the chance that susceptible unvaccinated people encounter the pathogen.

notes.A: Reduced exposure can indirectly protect the individual without directly converting their B cells into plasma cells.
notes.B: Unvaccinated people still rely on innate and adaptive defences when exposed.
notes.D: Population effects result from reduced transmission, not transfer of vaccine antigen between people.
notes.E: T-cell receptors remain those produced by the individual's own lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A vaccine shows strong efficacy in trials but reduced field effectiveness during a cold-chain failure. What best explains the difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of potency during programme delivery

options.label: B
options.text: A sudden loss of all antigen-specific receptors

questions.why: A break in recommended storage or transport conditions can damage a vaccine and reduce its potency. This can lower protection achieved in routine delivery despite high efficacy under controlled conditions.

notes.B: Exposure of stored doses to unsuitable temperatures does not imply that recipients have lost all antigen receptors.
notes.C: Stronger adjuvant activity is not the expected consequence of a cold-chain failure.
notes.D: Reduced potency reflects damage to the stored product rather than a need to invoke genetic changes in recipients.
notes.E: Lower coverage commonly reduces population protection and does not account for loss of potency during storage.

questions.stem: Which property most directly distinguishes a whole inactivated vaccine from a live attenuated one?

options.label: A
options.text: It contains no recognizable pathogen antigens

options.label: D
options.text: It contains organisms unable to replicate

options.label: E
options.text: It creates a self-replicating mRNA transcript

questions.why: The organisms in a whole inactivated vaccine retain antigenic material but cannot replicate. Live attenuated organisms retain limited replication capacity.

notes.A: The immune system can still recognise antigens on inactivated organisms.
notes.B: Replication competence is characteristic of the live attenuated option rather than a successfully inactivated preparation.
notes.C: Donor immunoglobulin is passive immunisation, with preformed antibodies rather than whole antigens.
notes.E: A self-amplifying RNA vaccine is a distinct platform from a whole inactivated organism.

questions.stem: Which platform presents self-assembled viral structural proteins without a replicating viral genome?
questions.why: A virus-like particle contains structural proteins assembled into a particle that resembles a virus. It presents antigenic surfaces without carrying a complete infectious viral genome.

notes.A: A live virulent virus has a genome capable of supporting infection.
notes.C: A whole inactivated bacterial vaccine contains nonreplicating bacteria, which are distinct from particles built from viral structural proteins.
notes.D: DNA repair enzymes have no defining role in this vaccine platform.
notes.E: Passive immunoglobulin supplies ready-made antibodies rather than particles that present antigen.

questions.stem: What is the principal immunizing material in a synthetic peptide vaccine?
questions.why: Synthetic peptide vaccines use defined short amino acid sequences derived from antigens. These sequences provide epitopes that can be recognised by the immune system.

notes.A: A bacterial chromosome is genetic material rather than a defined peptide antigen.
notes.B: Preformed donor antibodies confer passive protection.
notes.C: Live virus is a whole-organism vaccine platform rather than a synthetic peptide formulation.
notes.D: Host lymphocytes are immune cells, not the selected amino acid sequences that supply peptide epitopes.

questions.stem: How do mRNA-based vaccines provide antigen for immune recognition?

options.label: A
options.text: The mRNA converts directly into antibody

options.label: B
options.text: The mRNA integrates into host chromosomal DNA

options.label: D
options.text: The formulation contains intact virulent microbes

options.label: E
options.text: The mRNA acts only as a passive immunoglobulin

questions.why: Host ribosomes translate the delivered mRNA into antigen. Recognition of that antigen can then generate antibody and T-cell responses.

notes.A: mRNA is a set of instructions for making an antigen, rather than a molecule that turns into antibody.
notes.B: Translation occurs from RNA and does not require integration into the cell's DNA.
notes.D: An mRNA vaccine contains RNA encoding the antigen. It does not rely on delivery of intact virulent microbes.
notes.E: Passive immunoglobulin therapy supplies preformed antibodies. An mRNA vaccine stimulates the recipient's own response.

questions.stem: What is the main role of a viral vector in a vector-based vaccine?

options.label: A
options.text: Deliver genetic instructions for an antigen

options.label: B
options.text: Produce ready-made human IgG in the vial

questions.why: The vector delivers genetic information for an antigen. Antigen expressed by recipient cells then provides a target for the immune response.

notes.B: Ready-made IgG is administered in passive immunisation.
notes.C: Antigen presentation helps initiate the response and does not require wholesale destruction of presenting cells.
notes.D: Complement proteins are soluble immune effectors. They are not converted to RNA.
notes.E: Providing a limited genetic message does not entail replacing the recipient's genome.

questions.stem: Which vaccination strategy uses a weakened pathogen that can still replicate to a limited extent?
questions.why: Live attenuated vaccines use a weakened organism capable of limited replication. This exposure can stimulate active immunity while the organism's ability to cause disease is reduced.

notes.A: A whole inactivated organism lacks the ability to replicate.
notes.B: A toxoid is an inactivated toxin that retains useful antigenicity.
notes.C: A purified polysaccharide is an antigen component without a living organism.
notes.E: Passive infusion transfers antibodies rather than a pathogen capable of limited replication.

questions.stem: Which vaccination example generally involves a live attenuated oral preparation?
questions.why: Oral poliovirus vaccine contains live attenuated poliovirus, which can generate immunity at the intestinal mucosa. The injected inactivated poliovirus vaccine contains nonreplicating antigen.

notes.A: Inactivated polio vaccine is administered by injection and does not contain live attenuated virus.
notes.C: Tetanus vaccine contains a detoxified bacterial protein rather than an attenuated organism.
notes.D: Recombinant hepatitis B vaccine uses a viral surface antigen rather than a live organism.
notes.E: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine uses capsular polysaccharide linked to a carrier protein.

questions.stem: Which trial phase primarily establishes initial vaccine safety and tolerability in a small human group?
questions.why: Phase I usually studies a small group to obtain early evidence of safety, tolerability and sometimes immunogenicity in humans. Larger studies follow if the initial findings justify them.

notes.A: Phase II is a larger stage that explores dose and expands safety and immunogenicity data.
notes.B: Phase III is typically a large confirmatory stage that assesses protective efficacy and safety.
notes.C: Phase IV studies are conducted after a vaccine has been approved and introduced.
notes.D: Postmarketing surveillance begins after introduction, rather than providing the first safety evaluation in people.

questions.stem: Which development phase typically studies vaccine dose, immunogenicity and safety in hundreds of participants?
questions.why: Phase II usually expands enrolment to study dose and schedule while measuring immune responses and further characterising safety. It follows the smaller initial human evaluation.

notes.A: Phase I is usually smaller and emphasises initial safety and tolerability.
notes.B: Phase III is generally larger and commonly designed to test clinical efficacy.
notes.D: Phase IV occurs after approval and can assess safety or protection in routine use.
notes.E: The preclinical phase is undertaken before studies in human participants.

questions.stem: Which development phase generally tests vaccine efficacy and safety in thousands of trial participants?
questions.why: Phase III usually enrols enough participants to compare clinical outcomes and estimate protective efficacy. The larger sample also provides additional safety data.

notes.B: Phase I is designed primarily to assess initial safety and tolerability in a small group.
notes.C: Phase II is usually an investigation of dose, immune response and safety in a group larger than in Phase I.
notes.D: Phase IV occurs after authorisation rather than before initial approval.
notes.E: Candidate discovery is an early stage and does not measure protective efficacy in thousands of people.

questions.stem: Which phase includes monitoring after authorization and widespread vaccine use?
questions.why: Phase IV is postauthorisation study, when use in larger and more diverse populations can reveal rare adverse events and inform estimates of real-world protection. Broader safety surveillance also continues after introduction.

notes.A: Phase I is the initial human testing stage and generally involves only a small number of participants.
notes.B: Phase II is an earlier study of dose, immune responses and safety.
notes.C: Phase III is generally used to test efficacy and safety before authorisation.
notes.E: Proof of concept is an early milestone rather than postmarketing follow-up.

questions.stem: What is the main objective of the WHO Expanded Programme on Immunization?

options.label: B
options.text: Improve access to routine protective vaccination

options.label: C
options.text: Provide antibiotics for childhood viral infections

options.label: E
options.text: Increase routine use of antithrombotic medicines

questions.why: The WHO programme was established to expand access to routine vaccination against preventable diseases, initially with a focus on children. Its current remit supports equitable vaccination across the life course.

notes.A: Surveillance remains important for monitoring vaccine-preventable diseases, and vaccination is a preventive intervention.
notes.C: Antibiotics do not treat most childhood viral diseases and are not the programme's main intervention.
notes.D: Laboratory testing supports investigation and surveillance rather than being eliminated by vaccination.
notes.E: Antithrombotic medicines are used for clot-related indications, outside the programme's vaccination objective.

questions.stem: In what year was the WHO Expanded Programme on Immunization launched?
questions.why: WHO launched the Expanded Programme on Immunization in 1974. The aim was to extend protection from routine childhood vaccines globally.

notes.A: In 1964 the global programme had yet to be launched.
notes.B: The global programme was launched in 1974, five years after the date given in this option.
notes.C: Ghana's national programme was first implemented in 1978, following the global launch.
notes.D: The global programme was already operating by 1988.

questions.stem: In what year did Ghana adopt its Expanded Programme on Immunisation?
questions.why: Ghana Health Service dates the first national implementation of EPI to 1978. Ghana's programme followed the global initiative launched by WHO in 1974.

notes.A: The Ghanaian programme was not yet in operation in 1968.
notes.B: The year 1974 is the launch date of WHO's global programme, which preceded Ghana's first implementation.
notes.D: Ghana's national programme was already in operation by 1984, having started six years earlier.
notes.E: In 1998 the national programme had already been operating for about two decades.

questions.stem: What distinguishes eradication of infection from elimination in a defined region?

options.label: A
options.text: Eradication implies worldwide absence of the agent

options.label: B
options.text: Eradication means only low local disease prevalence

options.label: C
options.text: Elimination requires worldwide disappearance of the agent

options.label: D
options.text: Eradication describes temporary reductions in one city

options.label: E
options.text: Elimination indicates vaccine production has stopped

questions.why: Eradication is global disappearance of naturally occurring disease-agent transmission; elimination refers to interruption in a specified area.

questions.stem: A patient faints during vaccination because of injection-related fear. Which AEFI category best fits?
questions.why: Injection-related fear can trigger vasovagal syncope around vaccination. This fits the older anxiety-related AEFI category, now commonly addressed under immunisation stress-related responses.

notes.A: A product-related reaction is caused by inherent properties of a correctly manufactured and administered vaccine.
notes.B: A quality defect-related reaction involves a defect in the manufactured product or supplied device.
notes.C: An error-related reaction results from improper handling or administration, which is not described here.
notes.E: Malaria or another unrelated cause of fever can be coincidental, but this event is linked to procedural stress.

questions.stem: An unsterile needle used during vaccination transmits an infection. How is the event classified?
questions.why: An unsterile needle is an administration error. Infection attributable to that preventable lapse is an immunisation error-related reaction.

notes.A: A product-related reaction arises from the vaccine's inherent properties as supplied and used correctly.
notes.C: A vaccine quality defect originates in manufacture or the supplied product, rather than the described technique error.
notes.D: A stress-related response may include fainting but does not explain infection transmitted through equipment.
notes.E: A coincidental event is causally independent of vaccination, unlike an infection traced to a needle used for the injection.

questions.stem: A manufacturer fails to fully inactivate a vaccine batch, causing infection. Which category applies?
questions.why: Incomplete inactivation during manufacture is a defect in the batch. An infection caused by that faulty product is a vaccine quality defect-related reaction.

notes.A: A product-related reaction arises from inherent properties of a product that meets quality requirements.
notes.B: Procedural anxiety can cause a stress response but cannot explain infection from incomplete inactivation.
notes.C: A coincidental event has no causal relationship to the vaccine or vaccination process.
notes.D: An incorrectly scheduled dose is distinct from a defect introduced during manufacture.

questions.stem: A person develops malaria fever hours after vaccination; investigation finds no causal vaccine link. Which category applies?
questions.why: An adverse event following immunisation can occur near a vaccination in time without being caused by it. Malaria established as an independent cause makes the fever a coincidental event.

notes.A: A quality defect requires evidence of an issue with the manufactured product or supplied device.
notes.B: A product reaction is attributable to an inherent property of the vaccine.
notes.D: Administration errors involve failures such as improper handling or injection technique.
notes.E: An immunisation stress-related response can cause symptoms around the procedure but does not account for confirmed malaria.

questions.stem: What makes a monoclonal antibody preparation monoclonal?

options.label: B
options.text: Antibodies come only from normal serum

options.label: E
options.text: Antibodies originate from one B-cell clone

questions.why: A monoclonal preparation represents a single antibody-producing clone or a single cloned antibody design. Its molecules thus share defined antigen-binding specificity.

notes.A: Recognition of multiple unrelated targets by a mixture typically reflects different antibody populations rather than monoclonality.
notes.B: Ordinary serum contains antibodies from many different B-cell clones.
notes.C: A monoclonal antibody can retain constant domains, which contribute to isotype and effector function.
notes.D: The range of human isotypes does not determine whether the antibody population is clonal.

questions.stem: Compared with monoclonal antibodies, polyclonal serum antibodies characteristically:

options.label: B
options.text: Have no affinity for native proteins

options.label: C
options.text: Recognize multiple epitopes on an antigen

options.label: D
options.text: Are produced only in myeloma cells

questions.why: Polyclonal antibodies arise from many B-cell clones, each with its own binding specificity. Together they can recognise several epitopes on the same antigen.

notes.A: Uniform recognition of one epitope is typical of a conventional monoclonal reagent.
notes.B: Antibodies can bind exposed epitopes on native proteins.
notes.D: Polyclonal antibodies are produced by multiple antibody-secreting clones.
notes.E: The contributing clones have different rearranged antibody genes.

questions.stem: Which cellular fusion is used to produce conventional antibody-secreting hybridomas?

options.label: A
options.text: B cell fused with a myeloma cell

options.label: E
options.text: Platelet with a helper T lymphocyte

questions.why: Conventional hybridomas combine the antigen-specific antibody production of a B cell with the sustained capacity for growth of a myeloma cell. A single hybridoma clone can secrete monoclonal antibody.

notes.B: Macrophages are phagocytes and mature erythrocytes lack nuclei. Neither is an antibody-producing B cell.
notes.C: Dendritic cells and neutrophils have roles in defence but do not provide the required B-cell antibody specificity.
notes.D: NK cells and basophils are innate immune cells rather than sources of antibody secretion.
notes.E: Platelets and helper T cells do not secrete immunoglobulin.

questions.stem: What does HAT selection exploit during traditional hybridoma production?

options.label: A
options.text: De novo pyrimidine synthesis by unfused myeloma

options.label: C
options.text: Absence of thymidine in hybridoma medium

options.label: E
options.text: Direct mutation of each antibody epitope

questions.why: Aminopterin blocks folate-dependent de novo nucleotide pathways. A selected hybridoma can use salvage pathways supplied by the B-cell partner, allowing growth when the unfused salvage-deficient myeloma cannot proliferate.

notes.A: De novo production of critical nucleotides is blocked, preventing growth of the unfused salvage-deficient myeloma.
notes.B: Platelets have no role in providing antibody specificity or sustainable growth.
notes.C: Thymidine is one of the compounds provided in HAT medium for salvage.
notes.E: The selection tests metabolic capacity and continued growth rather than directly mutating antibody-binding sites.

questions.stem: A mouse antibody variable region is joined to human antibody constant regions. Which category is produced?
questions.why: The variable domains are mouse-derived while the constant domains are human. Combining domains from different species in this way is the classical chimeric design.

notes.A: Humanisation usually retains selected nonhuman antigen-binding loops within largely human variable frameworks.
notes.C: A fully human antibody has human-derived variable as well as constant regions.
notes.D: An unmodified mouse antibody has murine constant regions as well as variable regions.
notes.E: Polyclonal serum contains antibodies from multiple clones, rather than one defined design.

questions.stem: A therapeutic antibody retains only mouse-derived CDRs in an otherwise human framework. Which category fits?
questions.why: The complementarity-determining regions, or CDRs, supply much of the antigen-contact surface. Keeping murine CDRs in mainly human domains is a classical humanisation strategy.

notes.A: A classical chimera retains the entire nonhuman variable domains, including their frameworks.
notes.B: A fully murine antibody has mouse-derived frameworks and constant domains too.
notes.C: Polyclonal serum contains products of multiple B-cell clones rather than a defined CDR-grafted antibody.
notes.D: An unmodified anti-mouse antibody is described by what it targets, not by the grafted sequence architecture.

questions.stem: Which monoclonal antibody class contains exclusively human antibody-sequence components?
questions.why: A fully human monoclonal antibody has human-derived variable and constant regions. The human origin applies to its frameworks and antigen-contact sequences.

notes.A: A chimeric antibody has nonhuman variable domains combined with human constant domains.
notes.B: A humanised antibody can retain nonhuman antigen-binding loops.
notes.D: An unmodified murine antibody has mouse sequence across its antibody domains.
notes.E: A mouse–rabbit hybrid would contain components of nonhuman origin rather than solely human sequence.

questions.stem: Why are fully murine therapeutic antibodies more likely to provoke anti-drug immune responses?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater sequence foreignness to human immunity

options.label: D
options.text: Obligatory covalent binding to human DNA

options.label: E
options.text: Lack of disulfide bonds in all heavy chains

questions.why: Mouse antibody sequences can be recognised as foreign by a human recipient, leading to anti-drug antibodies. These responses can change drug clearance or reduce therapeutic activity.

notes.B: A functional murine antibody has variable regions that bind its target.
notes.C: Murine antibodies can recognise mammalian antigens if their specificity is appropriate.
notes.D: Covalent binding to human DNA is not an inherent property of therapeutic murine antibodies.
notes.E: Murine antibodies have disulfide bonds that contribute to immunoglobulin structure.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a naked monoclonal antibody drug?

options.label: A
options.text: An antibody carrying a cytotoxic drug

options.label: C
options.text: An antibody joining two cell receptors

options.label: E
options.text: An antibody lacking both Fab arms

questions.why: A naked monoclonal antibody has no attached drug, toxin or radionuclide. Its activity can come from direct target binding or recruitment of immune effector functions.

notes.A: An attached cytotoxic drug makes the product an antibody–drug conjugate.
notes.B: An attached radionuclide makes it a radiolabelled antibody.
notes.C: Binding two receptors describes target specificity. It does not establish whether the antibody carries a payload.
notes.E: Fab arms provide binding sites and can be present in an unconjugated antibody.

questions.stem: An anticancer monoclonal antibody carries a covalently attached cytotoxic compound. This is a:
questions.why: An antibody–drug conjugate links an antibody to a pharmacologically active drug payload. Antigen recognition can concentrate delivery to cells bearing the target.

notes.A: A naked antibody has no attached therapeutic payload.
notes.C: An unlabelled diagnostic antibody has no such attached cytotoxic compound.
notes.D: Polyclonal antitoxin serum is a mixture of antibodies intended to neutralise a toxin.
notes.E: Recombinant cytokines are signalling proteins rather than antibody–payload conjugates.

questions.stem: A monoclonal antibody binds two different target antigens at once. Which design is most likely?
questions.why: A bispecific antibody has binding sites with two different specificities. It can therefore engage two targets, unlike a conventional monospecific antibody.

notes.A: A polyclonal mixture can collectively bind different targets, but separate antibodies supply the different specificities.
notes.B: Class switching changes antibody constant regions and does not provide a second target specificity.
notes.C: Murine origin only describes the source of the antibody sequence.
notes.D: A single conventional Fab fragment has one antigen-binding site.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a radiolabelled monoclonal antibody from an unlabelled one?

options.label: B
options.text: Loss of all antibody disulfide bonds

options.label: D
options.text: Conversion to a B-cell receptor gene

options.label: E
options.text: Lack of a functional heavy chain

questions.why: A radiolabelled antibody carries a radionuclide that gives a detectable or therapeutic radiation signal. Its binding specificity can localise the signal to a target.

notes.A: Antigen binding is generally retained so the radiolabel can be localised to the desired target.
notes.B: Disulfide bond loss is not a defining property of a radioactive label.
notes.D: The labelled product is a protein conjugate, not a gene encoding a receptor.
notes.E: A radiolabelled antibody can have an intact heavy chain.

questions.stem: Which conventional therapeutic antibody name suffix traditionally indicated a humanized monoclonal antibody?
questions.why: In the older WHO naming system, the source substem in -zumab identified a humanised antibody. This convention is historical and should be applied to names assigned under that system.

notes.B: The older -omab ending indicated a mouse-derived antibody.
notes.C: The older -ximab ending indicated a chimeric antibody.
notes.D: The older -umab ending indicated a human antibody.
notes.E: The -cept stem is associated with receptor-based products, not the historical humanised antibody source substem.

questions.stem: Which conventional therapeutic antibody name suffix traditionally indicated a chimeric monoclonal antibody?
questions.why: In the older WHO naming system, -ximab identified a chimeric antibody. It described a design such as nonhuman variable domains and human constant domains.

notes.A: The older -omab ending is associated with a mouse-derived antibody rather than a chimeric antibody.
notes.B: The older -zumab ending referred to a humanised antibody.
notes.C: The older -umab ending referred to a human antibody.
notes.E: The -cept stem is used for some receptor-based products and is not the older chimeric antibody ending.

questions.stem: Which method tests patient red cells for immunoglobulin already attached to their surfaces in vivo?
questions.why: The direct antiglobulin test detects immunoglobulin or complement already attached to a patient's red cells in vivo. Antiglobulin reagent demonstrates that the sampled cells are coated.

notes.A: The indirect test detects serum antibodies that can bind red cells in vitro.
notes.C: Complement fixation assays detect complement consumption in an antigen–antibody reaction, rather than assessing the patient's own cell coating directly.
notes.D: Ouchterlony diffusion forms precipitin lines between soluble reagents in a gel.
notes.E: Competitive radioimmunoassay measures competition for binding and is not the method for detecting in vivo coated red cells.

questions.stem: Which method detects antibodies in patient serum by incubating them with reagent red cells in vitro?
questions.why: In the indirect antiglobulin test, serum antibodies are allowed to bind reagent red cells in vitro. Antiglobulin reagent then reveals antibodies that coated the reagent cells.

notes.A: The direct antiglobulin test is performed on patient cells that may already have been coated in vivo.
notes.B: Radial immunodiffusion measures a soluble antigen from the size of its precipitin ring.
notes.C: Radial immunodiffusion uses the size of a precipitin ring to measure soluble antigen in a sample.
notes.D: Neutralisation assays assess inhibition of a toxin's action and do not test serum against reagent red cells.

questions.stem: In a classical complement fixation test, what indicates that specific antibody has fixed complement to the test antigen?
questions.why: In a positive complement fixation test, antibody and test antigen consume available complement. Too little remains to lyse the sensitised indicator red cells, so lack of haemolysis is the positive endpoint.

notes.A: Lysis implies complement remained available, as expected in a negative test under valid control conditions.
notes.B: Fibrinogen is a coagulation protein and its production is not a readout of the assay.
notes.D: Direct fluorescence is used in other immunoassays rather than this complement-dependent haemolysis test.
notes.E: Labelled DNA fragments are readouts of some nucleic acid methods, not the classical fixation assay.

questions.stem: Which method detects a soluble antigen by attaching it to carrier particles that visibly aggregate with antibody?
questions.why: Passive agglutination uses antigen-coated particles to turn a soluble antigen–antibody reaction into visible clumping.

questions.stem: In reverse passive agglutination, what is attached to the carrier particles to detect soluble antigen?
questions.why: Reverse passive agglutination uses particles coated with capture antibody. A matching soluble antigen can link particles together through antigen–antibody binding and produce visible clumping.

notes.A: Antigen-coated particles are used in conventional passive agglutination to detect matching antibody.
notes.B: Messenger RNA is not the binding reagent used to capture antigen in this assay.
notes.C: The membrane attack complex can lyse susceptible targets but does not provide the specificity of a capture antibody.
notes.E: A protein kinase catalyses phosphorylation and is not the antigen-capture reagent.

questions.stem: In radial immunodiffusion, what happens as the amount of antigen applied to an antibody-containing gel increases?
questions.why: Antigen diffuses radially into gel containing antibody and precipitates where the two reach the necessary proportions. With the same sample volume and endpoint conditions, more antigen produces a wider ring, and its squared diameter can be related to concentration.

notes.A: Additional antigen normally shifts the position of the ring outward rather than causing instant disappearance.
notes.C: Antigen still spreads away from the well through the gel. Its diffusion does not reverse.
notes.D: The measurement is of ring diameter, which typically increases with antigen concentration under the assay conditions.
notes.E: Visible precipitation is due to antigen–antibody complexes, rather than covalent fluorescent labelling.

questions.stem: Which immunodiffusion method uses antigen and antibody in separate wells within a gel?
questions.why: In Ouchterlony double diffusion, soluble antigen and antibody diffuse from separate wells. A precipitin line forms where their local proportions permit extensive immune complex formation.

notes.A: Direct fluorescent staining uses a fluorescently labelled primary reagent to mark a target rather than forming diffusion lines in gel.
notes.B: Western immunoblotting uses a membrane to detect proteins already separated by electrophoresis.
notes.C: Radioimmunoassay uses a radioactive label to measure binding, rather than two sets of gel wells.
notes.D: Tube haemagglutination uses red-cell clumping as the readout.

questions.stem: Which test uses an enzyme-conjugated anti-human immunoglobulin to detect patient antibody bound to antigen-coated wells?
questions.why: The patient's antibody is the analyte. It binds immobilised antigen and is detected indirectly by an enzyme-labelled antibody directed against human immunoglobulin.

notes.A: A sandwich ELISA uses capture and detection antibodies to measure an antigen between them.
notes.B: The direct Coombs test measures immunoglobulin or complement already attached to the patient's red cells.
notes.D: A neutralisation assay measures inhibition of a biological effect rather than binding to an antigen-coated well.
notes.E: Rocket electrophoresis uses the height of an antigen–antibody precipitin peak, rather than an enzyme-labelled secondary antibody.

questions.stem: Which ELISA format detects antigen captured between two specific antibodies?
questions.why: The solid-phase capture antibody immobilises antigen, and a second antibody recognises another accessible site on that antigen. This two-antibody arrangement gives the sandwich format its name.

notes.B: An indirect antibody ELISA uses antigen on the solid phase and detects the bound sample antibody with a secondary antibody.
notes.C: A competitive ELISA uses competition for a limited number of binding sites rather than binding of antigen by two antibodies at once.
notes.D: The Coombs test uses antiglobulin reagent to detect coating of red blood cells.
notes.E: A Western blot detects protein bands after electrophoresis and transfer rather than capturing soluble antigen in an ELISA well.

questions.stem: In a competitive immunoassay, increasing patient antigen concentration typically produces which signal trend?

options.label: B
options.text: A signal independent of antigen concentration

options.label: E
options.text: Spontaneous conversion of antibody to DNA

questions.why: Unlabelled antigen from the sample competes with a labelled antigen for a limited number of antibody binding sites. More sample antigen leaves less labelled competitor bound, reducing the bound-label signal.

notes.A: More unlabelled antigen competes away labelled antigen, so signal from bound label falls.
notes.B: The assay depends on the signal changing with concentration when measured within its working range.
notes.C: Competition is due to binding and does not require damage to either antigen's epitopes.
notes.E: Antibodies are proteins and do not turn into DNA during the assay.

questions.stem: What distinguishes direct from indirect immunofluorescence in the detection step?
questions.why: In direct immunofluorescence, the antibody recognising the target carries the fluorophore. In indirect immunofluorescence, the labelled secondary antibody binds the primary antibody.

notes.A: DNA and RNA primers are nucleic acid reagents and do not distinguish the two antibody labelling formats.
notes.C: Rhodopsin is a visual pigment rather than the reagent that distinguishes direct from indirect antibody detection.
notes.D: Both formats can use monoclonal or polyclonal reagents. The distinction concerns which antibody carries the label.
notes.E: Cytokine or chemokine receptors can be targets of detection, but the identity of the target does not define the labelling format.

questions.stem: Which technique separates proteins by electrophoresis and identifies selected bands using specific antibodies?
questions.why: In Western immunoblotting, proteins are first separated and then transferred to a membrane. Antibodies reveal the separated bands corresponding to the target proteins.

notes.A: A Southern blot uses nucleic acid hybridisation to detect DNA fragments.
notes.B: A Northern blot uses a probe to identify RNA transcripts.
notes.C: Radial immunodiffusion measures a precipitin ring formed as antigen diffuses into antibody-containing gel.
notes.D: A complement fixation test uses complement consumption and an indicator system rather than separated protein bands.

questions.stem: An inexpensive rapid test uses antibody-coated membrane strips and capillary flow. Which method is illustrated?
questions.why: Lateral-flow immunochromatography uses capillary action to move a sample along a membrane. At designated lines, captured complexes form a visible or otherwise detectable signal.

notes.A: Rocket electrophoresis uses an electric field and forms precipitin peaks in a gel.
notes.B: Double immunodiffusion relies on diffusion from wells and forms precipitin lines in a gel.
notes.D: A radioimmunoassay uses a radioactive signal, rather than capillary flow through a membrane as its defining feature.
notes.E: Complement fixation is assessed by a complement-dependent indicator system rather than membrane capture lines.

questions.stem: Which older assay format uses a radiolabelled antigen competing against unlabelled analyte for limited antibody?
questions.why: Classical competitive radioimmunoassay measures competition between radiolabelled antigen and unlabelled analyte for antibody. The fraction of bound tracer can indicate the analyte concentration.

notes.B: Direct immunofluorescence uses a fluorophore on the antibody that binds the target.
notes.C: Passive latex agglutination uses clumping of coated particles as a visible readout.
notes.D: Ouchterlony immunodiffusion forms precipitin lines as antigen and antibody diffuse through gel.
notes.E: Direct antiglobulin testing uses antiglobulin reagent to detect coating of a patient's red cells.
